topic: Research: Agent Control Specification (ACS): Portable Runtime Governance for AI Agents Across Any Framework
keyword: Agent Control Specification ACS AI agent governance

key_points: Microsoft frames ACS as an open, vendor-neutral runtime governance standard for AI agents, independent of agent framework, runtime, or policy engine.
ACS defines eight intervention points: agent_startup, Input, pre_model_call, post_model_call, pre_tool_call, post_tool_call, output, and agent_shutdown.
Each policy check evaluates a host-provided runtime snapshot and can return allow, warn, deny, or escalate verdicts.
The canonical policy input includes intervention point, policy target, runtime snapshot, annotations from evidence providers, and tool metadata.
The article positions ACS as a response to fragmented framework-specific guardrails that are hard for security teams to audit centrally.
The Agent Governance Toolkit docs describe ACS as the decision-runtime core behind policy evaluation in AGT.
The manifest shape includes version, metadata, inheritance via extends, named policies, intervention_points, tool metadata, annotators, and approval configuration.
ACS supports a stateless information-flow control model where hosts supply provenance labels and manifests describe tool sink labels and clearances.
Telemetry is content-redacted by default and records decision metadata, reason codes, policy IDs, annotators, durations, and error classes rather than raw prompts or outputs.
SDK surfaces are documented for Python, Node.js, .NET, and Rust, with a normative specification path in the policy-engine package.
Microsoft Foundry presents ACS alongside ASSERT as an open trust stack for AI agents across frameworks.
The recommended loop is to use ASSERT to identify policy failures, apply ACS controls at checkpoints, and rerun ASSERT to validate improvement.
Microsoft says ACS has ecosystem support from governance, security, observability, and framework partners including Arize AI, IBM, CrewAI, KPMG, and Zscaler.
The article emphasizes that ACS controls should travel with the agent rather than being locked to a single infrastructure provider.
Observability integration is a competitive angle: policy decisions, approvals, and state transitions can be correlated with traces.
TechCrunch explains ACS for a broader developer audience as an open-source standard for granular control over what AI agents may do.
Policies can specify allowed actions, blocked actions, human approval triggers, and evidence to log for later review.
Policy files are checked at multiple interception points while the agent performs a task.
TechCrunch reports SDK or plugin support for LangChain, OpenAI Agents SDK, Anthropic Agents SDK, AutoGen, CrewAI, Semantic Kernel, Microsoft.Extensions.AI, MCP tools, and more.
The article's strongest angle is practical governance: moving controls out of prompts and one-off code into reusable policy files.
Aviatrix positions ACS as a single .guardrails.yaml policy file for declaring allowed tool surface, model constraints, and policy boundaries.
The article argues that in-process SDK guardrails are necessary but insufficient when compromised or jailbroken agents can still generate network traffic.
Aviatrix's differentiator is compiling the same ACS policy into multicloud network-layer enforcement across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and Kubernetes.
The post highlights blast-radius reduction, destination controls, protocol controls, identity controls, and policy enforcement on outbound connections.
This is useful as a contrarian section: ACS is a policy contract, but its value depends on enforcement layers around the agent runtime.

OWASP's Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 was developed with more than 100 industry experts, researchers, and practitioners to identify critical security risks facing autonomous and agentic AI systems.

Rubrik's 2026 agentic AI security survey of more than 1,600 IT and security leaders found 86% expect AI agents to outpace their organization's security guardrails within the next year, while only 23% report full visibility into agents operating in their environments.

McKinsey's 2026 AI trust research reports that 74% of respondents identify inaccuracy and 72% cite cybersecurity as highly relevant AI risks, with active mitigation lagging risk awareness across most categories.

The EU AI Act entered into force on August 1, 2024 and is generally fully applicable from August 2, 2026, with transparency rules coming into effect in August 2026 and some high-risk obligations extended to later dates.

Colorado's AI Act requires developers and deployers of high-risk AI systems, on and after February 1, 2026, to use reasonable care to protect consumers from known or reasonably foreseeable algorithmic discrimination risks.

angles: Explain ACS as policy-as-code for agents: a portable contract that security teams can review once and enforce across multiple frameworks.
Contrast ACS with prompt-based guardrails and framework callbacks; the key difference is standardized runtime intervention points and auditable verdicts.
Emphasize that ACS is not a magic safety layer: enforcement depends on host runtimes, SDK adapters, approval systems, telemetry, and sometimes network controls.
Use the eight intervention points as the article's practical spine, especially pre_tool_call and post_tool_call for tool misuse prevention.
Connect ACS to the enterprise control gap: agent deployments are growing faster than governance, auditability, identity management, and incident response.
Position ASSERT plus ACS as an evaluate-enforce-validate loop for teams moving agents from pilots into production.

Highlight the emerging stack boundaries: MCP standardizes tool access, A2A handles agent communication, OpenTelemetry/OpenInference handle traces, and ACS handles runtime permission and policy decisions.
Bring in regulated-industry relevance: ACS can help document policy decisions, approvals, evidence, and audit trails for finance, healthcare, legal, HR, and public-sector use cases.
Add a buyer's caveat: enterprises should ask which ACS intervention points a vendor actually supports, whether verdicts are fail-closed, and whether telemetry redacts sensitive content.
